Task 1 · Act I
Inventory and Initial Scan
Establishing the boundaries of the knowledge domain: what the archive contains, what it is missing, and what tools we bring to it.
Prepared for: Operations & Energy Steering Group
Domain: steel making, reheating furnace & hot rolling scheduling
Date: 16 September 2026

Executive Briefing
This report establishes the boundaries of the knowledge domain. It records what was
delivered, what survived de-duplication, what is missing, and what each surviving document actually
contains. Nothing here is interpreted yet. The purpose is to be able to say, with evidence, what the
organization currently knows and where that knowledge came from.

1. What was done
The archive arrived as loose PDFs with no index, no ordering and no statement of scope. The engineer
who assembled it left before documenting it. The first act therefore had to be mechanical before it
could be interpretive.
Automated text extraction.
Every PDF was converted to layout-preserving text
(
pdftotext -layout
), which preserves column structure and keeps tables readable.
Metadata extraction.
Title, author list, journal or proceedings, year, publisher keywords
and abstract were pulled from the front matter of each converted file.
Method and evidence extraction.
For each document the solution method, the objective
function and the validation evidence were read out of the methodology and results sections, not
inferred from the abstract. Reported figures were transcribed with their units.
De-duplication.
Matching on title and author list, not on filename, because the two
duplicate pairs arrived under different hashed filenames.
Manifest reconciliation.
The upload manifest was compared against files actually present.
Verification pass.
Every quantitative claim reproduced in this report set was traced back
to the sentence in the source document that states it.
Tools brought to the problem
Layout-preserving PDF text extraction; structured metadata capture into a single machine-readable
record per document; a seven-axis capability coding scheme applied uniformly across the corpus;
shared-anchor network construction; and a validated, colour-vision-safe visual system so that the
maps in Report 2 can be read by anyone. The corpus record is shipped as
data/corpus_metadata.csv
so the analysis can be rerun or challenged.
2. Boundaries of the knowledge domain
The archive is not a random pile. Read as a whole it defines a domain with four hard edges.
Inside the boundary
The energy-intensive thermal stage of steel making.
Reheating furnaces, soaking pits,
heat-treatment and quench-and-temper lines, forging furnaces. This is where the archive is thickest.
Scheduling as the control lever.
Almost every document treats the sequence and timing of
work, not the equipment design, as the thing to change. Capital investment is explicitly out of scope
in several of them.
Uncertainty as a first-class citizen.
Machine breakdown, uncertain release times, uncertain
gas calorific values, uncertain processing times, unpredictable order arrival.
The plant-level energy system.
By-product gas, steam, on-site generation, and the
electricity market the plant buys from and sells into.
The human who has to accept the schedule.
A late but distinct arrival in the archive.
Outside the boundary
Combustion and furnace design.
CFD, burner geometry and heat-transfer modelling appear only
as cited background, never as contributions.
Metallurgy of the product.
Grade design, microstructure and mechanical properties are
treated as constraints to satisfy, not as variables to optimise.
Supply chain beyond the plant gate.
One document reaches to a division-wide order book;
none reach further.
Process safety.
One manifest entry pointed at it. That file never arrived, so the domain as
delivered has no safety dimension at all.
Corpus by year and cluster
28 documents, 2016-2026. Furnace and uncertainty work runs throughout;
digital-twin and explainability work is almost entirely post-2022.

The gap matters and should be closed. Two of the three missing titles sit directly on the domain's
main axis: one on hot rolling scheduling optimisation, one on simulation-based multi-criteria
optimisation. The third, on process safety and artificial intelligence, is the only document that
would have given the archive a safety perspective on autonomous scheduling. Its absence is the single
largest known hole in the evidence base and should be treated as an open action, not a footnote.

3.3 Provenance signal
Several PDFs carry download stamps from Universidad Politecnica de Madrid dated 2 and 3 July 2026,
and one carries a Wiley stamp routed through a Spanish national provision. The archive was therefore
assembled in a single burst from an academic subscription, not accumulated over time from vendor
documentation or internal studies. Practically, this means the corpus is a literature scan rather
than an operational knowledge base. It contains almost no plant-specific data, no equipment
specifications and no cost baselines from this organization. That distinction shapes everything that
follows: the archive tells us what is possible, not what is currently true here.

7. Initial observations carried into Report 2
The corpus is bimodal in time.
Everything before 2021 is optimisation of a well-posed
scheduling problem. Everything after 2022 adds a model of the world (a twin) or a model of the user
(explainability). These are not refinements of the earlier work. They are a different research
programme that happens to share a problem domain.
Energy is measured in at least four incompatible units across the corpus:
minutes of
furnace time, GJ per tonne, currency per shift, and megawatts exported. No two documents can be
compared on energy without a conversion the authors never supply.
Validation depth varies by an order of magnitude.
One document validates against 161,109

The six tensions
Tension 1. Provable optimality against decision speed

These results do not degrade. They are true of the plant on its worst day.
Ship it
P11
reports its learned dispatcher running
roughly 100× faster than

on the static problem and
more than 20× faster than ALADIN
, while
staying within
0.3%
of ALADIN's solution quality.
P17

mill while it is moving.
P19

large enough that mixed-integer programming is hard to deploy online at all.
What it costs.
P23's exact algorithm caps out at
80 slabs
. A real rolling unit
in P02 runs
100 to 500 slabs
. Provable optimality is therefore not merely slower at plant
scale; for the integrated problem it is unavailable. Meanwhile P11's 0.3% quality gap is smaller than
the measurement error on most plant energy meters.
The decision.
Not "exact or heuristic" but
where the audit line sits
. The exact
methods are too slow to run the plant and too valuable to discard, because they are the only way to
know how much a fast method left behind. Treat them as the reference standard, not the controller.
Tension 2. Model abstraction against physical fidelity
How much furnace physics does a scheduler actually need to carry?
Abstract the machine
The dominant convention, traceable to Mouzon and carried by
P25
and
P26
,
reduces a machine to a few discrete modes with fixed transition costs.
P26
goes further and
removes the energy term from the objective entirely, replacing it with a single structural
constraint: no machine may idle. It is cheap to model, cheap to solve, and it scales to 200 jobs on
8 machines.
Model the physics
P04
argues directly against the convention: a static transition graph "might be
too restrictive for some types of machines (e.g. the furnaces)". It replaces the mode set with
continuous time-domain dynamics and derives the energy-optimal control law by Pontryagin's minimum
principle. Across 6750 instances the physics model
dominates the 600 °C, 700 °C
and combined transition graphs at every utilisation band
, and at low utilisation its average idle
power is
less than half
theirs.
P18
supplies the harder evidence. Its three-stage furnace twin holds
relative error under
0.98%
against real charging and discharging times.
What it costs.
Fidelity costs system identification, instrumentation and
maintenance. But P18 reports the result that settles the argument: run the same tabu search, ALNS and
hybrid metaheuristics
without
the high-fidelity twin and the resulting schedules are sometimes
worse than the manual schedules they were meant to replace
. An optimiser fed a wrong model
optimises confidently in the wrong direction.
The decision.
Fidelity is not a refinement to add in phase three. It is a gate. Until
the twin is validated, algorithmic sophistication is a liability, not an asset.
Tension 3. Energy as constraint, objective, proxy or price
The archive uses the word energy four incompatible ways. Which one governs?
Energy as structure or proxy
P26
never computes energy in the objective. It forbids idle machine time and
reports
29.57% energy saved for a 0.12% makespan increase
— the best energy return per
unit of production disruption anywhere in this corpus.
P23
,
P18
and
P01
use proxies: total rolling start times, makespan, furnace
working time. P01 reports furnace time cut by
12, 21 and 30 minutes
across three batches and
calls it energy saving without measuring a joule.
Energy as objective or price
P24
puts natural gas cost directly in a bi-objective model and reports
energy cost down 13% and tardiness down 90%
.
P10
quantifies ladle baking and start-up
energy explicitly and gets
1.21%
at constant productivity.
P05
predicts heat energy per
tonne in
GJ/t
to
94.7%
accuracy.
P19
,
P22
,
P11
and
P12
go further and treat energy as a price. P11
reports operating cost
57.4% below manual scheduling
. P12 measures success in exported
megawatts and gas flared.
What it costs.
These four framings produce different schedules for the same plant.
A proxy objective can be satisfied while energy rises: shortening furnace residence time reduces
holding loss but can force colder charging and higher heating demand, and no proxy-based document in
this archive measures that. Conversely P26 shows a pure constraint can outperform an explicit
objective on returns.
The decision.
Use all three, in a fixed precedence. Constraints where the physics gives
a free win (no-idle, holding limits). An explicit metered objective in GJ/t where the trade-off is
genuine. Price only at the layer that is actually exposed to the market. What must stop is the
uncontrolled substitution of proxies for measurements.
Tension 4. Plan, protect, react or learn
Disruption is certain. Should the schedule absorb it, be rebuilt around it, or be replaced by a policy?
Protect the plan
P07
builds a baseline that can absorb a breakdown: it pre-compresses processing
times so the realised schedule can match up with the plan. Against the plant's manual method it cuts
expected rescheduling cost from
50,600 to 47,592
and reduces the number of disrupted jobs from
six to four.
P23
optimises the worst case under budgeted uncertainty and makes no distribution
assumptions.
P06
carries uncertainty as fuzzy numbers through to a Pareto front.
React, or learn a policy
P09
does not protect anything. It classifies the disturbance and matches a
response: minor timing drift absorbed by transport flexibility, machine changes handled by local
exchange, large events by full reschedule. Over 24 hours, 90 charges and 18 plan changes it cut the
standard deviation of ladle turnover from
40.82 to 14.79 minutes
.
P19
and
P22
abandon the schedule object entirely and learn a policy that maps
observed state to action.
What it costs.
P23
concedes its own weakness: budgeted uncertainty is
conservative, and the authors name reduced conservatism as future work.
P08
names the opposite
failure: high-frequency rescheduling destroys production stability, which is why it forecasts release
times rather than reacting to them.
The decision.
P09's architecture is the resolution and it is the most transferable
single idea in the archive. Do not choose one response.
Choose a response policy
that grades
the reaction to the size of the disturbance, so small events never trigger a plant-wide replan.
Tension 5. Accuracy against explainability
If the best schedule cannot be explained, is it the best schedule?
Accuracy first
P14
states the orthodox position, citing Gunning and Aha: the most accurate
methods are frequently the least explainable, and the most explainable methods exhibit lower accuracy.
On that reading, explainability is a tax paid in performance.
Twenty-one documents in this corpus implicitly accept it. They optimise, report the gain, and never
address who will accept the result.
Acceptance first
P15
supplies the number that breaks the orthodoxy. In the PPC survey it cites,
only 19% of respondents said their planning system's schedules were accepted and not overridden
,
and just
35%
expressed confidence in the results. A schedule that is overridden delivers none
of its modelled savings, however optimal it was.
P16
shows the same principle paying: putting the operator in the loop with dynamic break
integration cut downtime
42.6%
and raised productivity
23.9%
.
What it costs.
Less than the orthodoxy claims. Every explanation method in this
archive is
post hoc
: P13 explains a genetic algorithm's selection, crossover and mutation with
decision trees after the fact; P15 attaches a SHAP Deep Explainer to a trained PPO policy; P21 runs
NSGA-II counterfactual search over an already-built MILP schedule. None of them changes the optimiser.
The accuracy cost of post-hoc explanation is
zero
. The real cost is interface work and
operator time.
The decision.
The trade-off as usually stated is a false one. Treat explainability as
an acceptance requirement with an engineering cost, not as a performance concession. On P15's numbers
it is the cheapest available multiplier on every other investment in this report.
Tension 6. Local optimum against system optimum
Which couplings do we integrate, and which do we deliberately leave alone?
Decompose
Most of the archive optimises one stage. It is defensible: decomposition is what makes
these problems solvable at all, and P23's exact method already caps at 80 slabs on a single stage.
Every additional coupling multiplies the state space.
Integrate
P02
shows separation costs real money: optimising reheating furnace scheduling and
the rolling plan jointly beats optimising them separately on
both
objectives at once, across
all 11 real instances.
P10
integrates production scheduling with ladle dispatching for
1.21%
energy at constant productivity.
P27
names the obstacle directly —
"information silos" between hot and cold rolling — and
P17
names the institutional
version, an automation hierarchy in which the ERP layer "only rarely has access to any process related
information".
What it costs.
P21
gives the sharpest warning, and it comes from the
explainability cluster rather than the scheduling one: improving one operation's processing time can
worsen
the makespan of the whole schedule. Its counterfactual search refuses to report any
improvement that does not also improve the system. Local optimisation is not merely incomplete. It
can be actively harmful.
The decision.
Integrate where stages share a
temperature
, because that is where
the physics couples: furnace to rolling, ladle to converter, hot rolling to cold rolling. Leave
couplings that share only a calendar decomposed. This is a sharper rule than "integrate everything"
and it is the one the evidence supports.

Task 4 · Act III
Integrative Synthesis
One unified blueprint: the learning and twin advances combined with the metallurgical constraints, and the explainability work put where it earns its cost.
Prepared for: Operations & Energy Steering Group
Domain: steel making, reheating furnace & hot rolling scheduling
Date: 16 September 2026
Report 3 left six tensions, five of which resolve toward layering rather than
selection. This report performs the act of integration: it combines the theoretical advances of the
learning and twin clusters with the practical constraints of the metallurgical cluster, and puts the
explainability cluster where it can actually do work. The output is a reference architecture that
could be built, with each component traced to the document that justifies it.
1. Design principles
Six principles fall out of Acts I and II. Each is stated as a rule, with the evidence that forces
it. They are ordered by precedence: where two conflict, the lower number wins.
Fidelity gates optimisation.
No optimiser is connected to production until the model it
optimises against has been validated against real charging, discharging and heating times. P18 showed
the same metaheuristics producing schedules worse than manual scheduling when the twin was absent.
The gate is quantitative: P18 achieved under 0.98% relative error, so under 1% is the acceptance
threshold.
Energy is constrained first, metered second, priced third.
Free structural wins are taken
as constraints (P26: 29.57% for 0.12%). Genuine trade-offs are made against a metered GJ/t objective
(P05, P24). Only the layer actually exposed to the market optimises against price (P11, P19). Proxies
are never substituted for measurement without a documented conversion.
Response is graded to disturbance.
P09's three-tier scheme — absorb, exchange,
reschedule — is adopted as the plant's rescheduling policy, because P08 shows that reacting to
everything destroys production stability.
Explanation is post hoc and mandatory.
Every decision surface produces an explanation from
a method that does not modify the optimiser (P13, P15, P21). Explanation is an acceptance
requirement, not a performance concession.
Integrate across shared temperature, decompose across shared calendar.
Furnace to rolling
(P02), schedule to ladle (P10), hot to cold rolling (P27). Everything else stays decoupled.
Keep a provable reference.
The exact and competitive-ratio methods (P04, P03, P23) are
retained off-line as the audit standard, so the organization can always quantify what the fast layer
gave up.

5. Implementation sequence
Phase 1 — Instrument and constrain (months 0–6).
Build the L0 constraint register and the L2 energy-per-tonne meter. Apply the no-idle and holding-time
constraints to the existing manual schedule with no optimiser involved. This phase needs no AI, and
on P26's evidence it is where the highest energy return per unit of disruption sits. Exit criterion:
metered GJ/t reporting in production, and the constraint register signed off by metallurgy.
Phase 2 — Build and gate the twin (months 4–12).
Construct the L1 three-stage furnace twin and validate it against historical production. Run L3's
shift tier in shadow mode against it.
Do not connect the optimiser to production until relative
error is below 1%.
Exit criterion: the twin reproduces last quarter's charging and discharging
times within the gate, and shadow schedules beat the executed ones on the L2 meter.
Phase 3 — Decide and explain together (months 9–18).
Switch on the L3 tiers behind the L5 explanation layer, and instrument the override rate from day one.
Add L4 only once the production side is stable, because market exposure amplifies the cost of a wrong
schedule. Exit criterion: override rate trending down, and the nightly audit showing the fast tiers
within a stated percentage of the exact reference.
Phase 1 and Phase 2 overlap deliberately. Phase 3 does not start before Phase 2 clears its gate,
because P18's result makes starting early actively harmful.

Task 5 · Act III
From furnace heat to a decision
Executive briefing for the Operations and Energy Steering Group. Twenty-eight documents, six trade-offs, one blueprint, three decisions.
Prepared for: Operations & Energy Steering Group
Domain: steel making, reheating furnace & hot rolling scheduling
Date: 16 September 2026
This briefing converts 28 documents into one decision. It is written for the steering
group, it assumes no familiarity with the source literature, and every number in it is traceable to a
named document in the accompanying reports.
The briefing in one paragraph
Reheating consumes 15 to 20% of this plant's total energy and 60 to 70% of all energy used in
rolling. The published evidence says scheduling alone can take a double-digit percentage off that
without capital investment. It also says two things we are not currently set up for: an optimiser
running on an unvalidated model produces schedules
worse than the ones people write by hand
,
and roughly four planning-system schedules in five get overridden by the people who have to run them.
The recommendation is a three-phase, eighteen-month programme that fixes the model before it deploys
the optimiser, and builds the explanation alongside the decision rather than after it.
A — Attention
We are paying for heat we do not need
The furnace is not one cost among many. On the evidence assembled in Report 1, it is the cost.
15–20%
of total energy in iron and steel production goes to the reheating furnace (P05)
60–70%
of all energy used in the rolling process goes to the same stage (P05)
up to 70%
of hot-rolling process energy is ingot heating, at 2–2.4 GJ per tonne (P06)
80%
of a machine's total energy can be consumed while it sits idle (P26)
Three consequences follow, and they are uncomfortable in sequence.
The single largest controllable energy cost in the plant is a sequencing decision
, not an
equipment decision. Every document in this archive that saves energy saves it by changing the order
and timing of work.
We are almost certainly not measuring it.
The archive shows that most plants optimise
furnace
time
and describe the result as energy saving without ever computing a joule. Report 3
shows the two can move in opposite directions.
The window is closing on doing nothing.
Steel accounts for about 8% of global energy demand
and 7% of energy-sector carbon emissions, and the International Energy Agency's roadmap requires those
emissions to at least halve by 2050 (P19). Energy price exposure and emissions exposure now move
together.
The number that should worry us most is not an energy number.
In the
production-planning survey cited by P15, only
19%
of respondents said their planning system's
schedules were accepted and not overridden, and only
35%
had confidence in its results. A 13%
energy saving that gets overridden four times in five is a 2.5% energy saving.

Three capabilities have become real in the last four years
Report 1's timeline shows a field mid-transition. Digital twins and explainable AI barely appear
before 2022 and dominate the recent literature. What changed is that both are now validated on real

The usual objection to this programme is that it hands control of an expensive, high-temperature,

## Headline findings

1. **The corpus is bimodal in time.** Pre-2021 work optimises a well-posed scheduling
   problem. Post-2022 work adds a model of the world (digital twin) or a model of the
   user (explainability). These are different research programmes sharing a domain.

2. **The optimisation core is mature and well connected.** 21 of 28 documents carry real
   metallurgical or thermal physics; a small set of anchor works ties the field together.

3. **Model fidelity is a gate, not a refinement.** P18 showed the same metaheuristics
   producing schedules *worse than manual scheduling* when run without a validated twin.

4. **Energy is defined four incompatible ways across the corpus** - as a constraint, an
   explicit objective, a time proxy, and a market price - and they produce different
   schedules for the same plant.

5. **The critical intersection is empty.** Zero documents combine an explicit energy
   objective with explainability. Not sparse. Zero. The seven explainability documents
   contain no steel at all.

6. **Acceptance, not accuracy, is the binding constraint.** In the survey cited by P15,
   only 19% of planning-system schedules were accepted without override.

## Method note

Text was extracted with layout-preserving PDF conversion. Metadata, solution methods,
objective functions and validation evidence were read from the methodology and results
sections of each document rather than inferred from abstracts; every quantitative claim
reproduced in the reports was traced to the sentence that states it. Network edges are
shared methodological anchors (same foundational citation, formalism or algorithmic
primitive), not topical similarity and not direct citation.

Figures use a categorical palette validated for colour-vision deficiency
(adjacent-pair CVD dE 9.1 light / 8.4 dark, normal-vision dE 19.6 / 19.3). Identity is
carried by shape, position and direct labels as well as by colour, and every figure has
a corresponding table or CSV.

- 31 files listed in the upload manifest, 28 unique documents received.

  safety and artificial intelligence. That absence is the largest known hole in the
  evidence base and is carried as an open action in Report 4's risk register.
